title: Enemies Turned Business Partners: Israelis and Palestinians Build Startups Together
summary: Imagine waking up to soldiers in your house when you're just 11. That happened to Salah Hussein, a Palestinian from Nablus. For years, he was scared of anyone in an Israeli uniform. But now, at 33, he's chosen to work with an Israeli partner. They're building a business together. Salah is part of 50:50 Startups, a program where Israelis and Palestinians team up to create new companies. They spend six months in workshops and get help from mentors. Then they go to Boston to pitch their ideas to investors. Salah's team, Qanara Tech, is making AI cameras that spot bugs in greenhouses before they ruin crops. His co-founder is Yana Shaulov, a 37-year-old Israeli scientist. She grew up in a mixed neighborhood and believes living together is the only way. "It's not always easy," she says. "But we're both here to stay." Other teams are building a better heart monitor and a water filter made from eggshells and seeds. It's not simple. Starting a business is hard—90% fail. And here, partners also face anger from people back home who think they shouldn't work with "the enemy." Salah sometimes hears a voice in his head calling him a "normalizer." But he pushes back: "Keep going! Tiny effects can lead to change." At a recent event, a French Israeli woman told a Palestinian participant about being attacked with a knife years ago. It was tense, but they kept talking. The program shows that even small steps can build bridges.
why_it_matters: This story shows that even when people have big disagreements, finding something to work on together can build trust and new ideas—just like teaming up with someone you don't usually get along with for a school project.

background_read: Israelis and Palestinians have a long, painful conflict over land in the Middle East, but some people try to build peace by working together on everyday projects.
Boston is a major city in the United States, famous for its universities and many investors who fund new technology companies.
Nablus, where Salah comes from, is a Palestinian city in the West Bank—a territory where many Palestinians live under Israeli military control and face checkpoints.
Article_Structure: WHO: Israeli and Palestinian entrepreneurs like Salah Hussein (from Nablus) and Yana Shaulov (an Israeli scientist).
WHAT: They join 50:50 Startups, a program that helps them create companies like Qanara Tech, which builds AI cameras to detect bugs in greenhouses.
WHERE: Workshops take place in Israel and the Palestinian territories, then they pitch their ideas to investors in Boston, USA.
WHY: To prove that even small steps of cooperation can open doors to economic opportunity and slowly chip away at deep mistrust.

perspectives.description: Supporters believe that when Israelis and Palestinians run businesses together, fear and anger can turn into friendship and peace.
Some people back home call the partners 'normalizers' and say it's wrong to cooperate while the conflict and occupation continue.
Business experts note that most startups fail anyway, so the real value might be the conversations and relationships, not just the companies.
